output:
Here's the letter — printed-and-posted version, with the address block at the top so it looks properly like a letter and not a long text message.

---

**Kelechi Obi**
**[Flat / house number]**
**Croydon**
**[Postcode]**

**6 November 2026**

---

Kelechi,

Right. You said if I was serious, I should put it in writing. So here it is. A letter, on paper, in an envelope, going through a sorting office in south London and out to Croydon by van and postman. If the man delivering it asks what it is, tell him it's a proposal, not a ransom. Actually don't tell him anything, he'll just hand it over and that will be the most exciting thing that's happened to him all week.

Let me get the easy bit out of the way first, because I know how your brain works. I'm not asking you to quit your job tomorrow. I'm not asking you to apply for anything. I'm not even asking you to decide by Christmas. I'm asking you to come to an open evening on **Thursday 19 November, 6pm**, at the training partnership in Lewisham. Come with me. Look at it. If it's rubbish, tell me it's rubbish and buy me food for lying to you.

That's the whole ask. Everything else in this letter is just me explaining why I think you'd be good at it, and being honest with you about the parts that are rubbish.

**Start with the bit you already know.**

On my birthday you were doing the thing where you complain about the job but make it funny, and then underneath the joke you said something that wasn't funny at all. Nine years. Same spreadsheet. Same Monday. And then I said you should come and teach maths, and you laughed like I'd suggested you should swim to Lagos, and you said: put it in writing.

So I'm putting it in writing. I'm serious about the open evening. That's it.

**Why you, specifically.**

You got an A in further maths. I remember it. You were in Moremi with your notes organised like a military operation, and half that hostel would not have passed without you. You tutored me, actually — I still remember you explaining surds to me at about 2am with jollof rice in your hand, because somebody's mother was cooking at midnight and the whole corridor smelled like it. You were patient with people who were slower than you, which is the single rarest thing in the world, because everyone is patient with people who are quick.

Christmas, though. My nephew. Fractions. You put portions of jollof rice onto plates and made him do the fractions. He is nine years old. He still brings it up. He still asks for the plate method. Do you understand what that means? A child who doesn't want to do maths asks for *more* maths. That's not me being sentimental, that's the whole job in one Christmas afternoon.

And you're funny. Genuinely funny, in a way that works with teenagers, because they can tell the difference between a teacher who is being funny and a teacher who is trying to sound young. They would like you. They would trust you. And you have that thing where you explain something without making anybody feel stupid — which, for the record, I never managed as a student and I'm still working on it as a teacher.

Then there's the other thing you said, on your birthday, which you probably remember better than I do: *I just want to do something that matters before 40.* You're 34, Kelechi. That's about five years. I'm not going to stand here and tell you teaching maths is the answer to life. But I'm telling you that checking other people's costings for nine years is not going to be the answer to that question. You already asked it. You already know.

**What the job actually looks like.**

Our school in Peckham has about 1,100 kids on roll. Since September we have had a supply teacher covering **two** Year 9 maths groups — so around sixty Year 9s who are not really getting taught maths properly, and who are getting two sets of supply cover while someone looks for a permanent post. I want to be clear that this is the situation I'm describing from the inside, and I'm describing it because it's exactly the kind of thing that eats me up. That is why I am asking you to come and look at a training route rather than a job advert.

The route is the **salaried** one. One year of training, you start September 2027, and you are paid while you train. The pay does drop in the first year. I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. It hurts, and I won't pretend to you otherwise, because you'd see it coming in the first month and you'd never trust a word I said again. But there is holiday pay, there is a pension, and it goes up after that. It isn't flat. And it isn't the same spreadsheet every single day of the year.

**The bad parts, honestly, because you won't believe the good parts otherwise.**

- Marking is endless. I mark on Sunday evenings sometimes. There will be more marking than you expect and less time to do it than you'd like.
- Behaviour is wahala on some days. There will be a lesson where the class is a wall and nothing you say is landing, and you will walk out and think *what am I doing.* Some days teaching is the loneliest thing you have ever done.
- The paperwork will bore you more than spreadsheets bore you now. I am not joking about that. Nobody warns you about the paperwork.
- Some of these kids' home situations will break your heart a little, and there is no module for that.

Also — and I'm saying this so you don't picture me bouncing in — I'm not romanticising it. I cried in the car park twice in the first term when I started in 2019. Twice. I am not hiding it because I don't want to sell you something I haven't lived. But that was the hardest year of my life and it did get better. By the second term I wasn't crying. By the third term I was laughing in the staff room with the other teachers about the Year 9s, and the thing that had changed was that I could see I was *useful.*

**The good part.**

Last month, a Year 11 boy called Damola finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks of being stuck. It clicked, and he shouted **"IS THAT ALL?!"** — like he was personally offended it was that simple — and the whole class clapped, and he stood there glowing. And I thought about you, Kelechi, because that is precisely the feeling half of Moremi hostel used to get. You didn't teach them maths. You made them feel like maths was something they were allowed to be good at.

And you're not too old, before you build that excuse. A woman in my department started at 41. She's one of the best teachers in the building and the kids would go through walls for her.

**So: the 19th of November.**

Six o'clock, Lewisham. It's an open evening — they show you the programme, you meet the people who run it, you get to ask the awkward questions, including the ones about money and workload that I know are already sitting in your head. I'll come with you. I'll introduce you. You won't have to talk to a single stranger alone.

Applications for next September open soon, which is why the date is soon. If you come on the 19th and it makes sense to you, you can apply while it's still fresh. If it doesn't, I'll never bring it up again — I'll bring it up at your birthday, once, every two years, like a Nigerian aunty, and then I'll stop.

Come to the open evening, Kelechi. That's the only thing I'm asking. One evening. Bring questions, bring your doubts, bring the spreadsheet brain — actually bring the spreadsheet brain, because you need it, there's paperwork.

Right, I have to go and mark about ninety pieces of coursework so I don't have to do it on Sunday.

Love,

**[Your name]**

---

*P.S. — I have deliberately not written down how much I think you'd be good at this, because you'd have accused me of exaggerating and then used it as evidence that I was exaggerating. Just come and look.*

---

A few notes on what I did with your points, so you can adjust before you print:

- **The bad parts** are grouped in a bullet list on purpose. It reads as more credible than burying them in prose, and it looks like you're not hiding anything.
- **The car park / "it gets better"** is placed *after* the bad bits rather than before, so it lands as evidence rather than as a sales pitch.
- **The jollof rice fractions** and **Moremi at 2am** are the two strongest "only you could do this" details, so I gave them the most space.
- **"Come to the open evening"** is repeated three times deliberately, because he will read this once on the train and think about it for a week. The letter doesn't ask him to apply — only to come.
- I left the address and sign-off as placeholders since I don't have his address or your name.
